title: The unorganised sector: ninety per cent of India at work
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Most Indian workers have no written contract, no provident fund and no pension. What e-Shram tries to change.
body:
India's workforce is overwhelmingly **informal**. According to official labour force surveys and studies by the ILO, the great majority of workers are in the unorganised sector or in informal jobs, including informal jobs inside formal firms. A worker in this position typically has no written contract, no provident fund, no pension and no paid leave. When illness, an accident or old age comes, there is nothing between the worker and hardship. This post looks at who these workers are, how many there are, how the State has tried to count and cover them, and where BMS stands.

## How big is the unorganised sector?

The Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act, 2008 describes the unorganised sector as a production or service enterprise owned by individuals or self-employed workers and, if it hires workers, employing fewer than ten. The organised sector is everything else, though even organised enterprises can employ unorganised workers. According to the National Sample Survey's 66th round for 2011-12, unorganised workers made up about 88 per cent of a labour force of about 47.29 crore. A committee report of 2012 placed the share of the unorganised or informal sector at over 90 per cent of the workforce.

More recent studies point in the same direction. The India Employment Report 2024, prepared by the Institute for Human Development and the ILO, says that around 90 per cent of Indian workers are in informal work and that the share of regular employment, which had been rising since 2000, started falling after 2018. The Periodic Labour Force Survey for 2023-24 shows that 58.4 per cent of workers were self-employed, including unpaid family helpers, while only 21.7 per cent were regular wage or salaried employees. The overall unemployment rate in that survey was 3.2 per cent. That low figure does not tell us about the quality of work, since a person who sells vegetables on a cart or does piece-rate work at home counts as employed.

## Who they are

The unorganised sector is not one group. It includes:

- street vendors and hawkers,
- home-based workers, such as those who stitch, roll beedis or pack goods at home,
- construction workers and brick-kiln workers,
- agricultural labourers,
- domestic workers,
- rag pickers and waste workers,
- handloom, handicraft and other craft workers,
- gig and platform workers, who are a newer addition.

The word that BMS uses for the self-employed craftsperson, whether potter, weaver, carpenter, blacksmith or cobbler, is the **Vishwakarma sector**. These are people who own a few tools and little else, and who do not fit easily into either the "employer" or the "employee" box in the law.

## Why work is so insecure

The India Employment Report gives a hint of the problem. It says that in 2022, 62 per cent of unskilled casual agricultural workers and 70 per cent of unskilled construction workers did not receive the minimum daily wage prescribed for them. The reason is not that the law is absent. A minimum wage exists on paper, but when workers are scattered, have no records and no union, there is nobody to check. This is why unions have long argued that the first step is not another scheme but proof that the worker exists.

## e-Shram: counting the uncounted

In August 2021 the Ministry of Labour and Employment launched the **e-Shram portal**, India's first Aadhaar-seeded national database of unorganised workers. The Ministry's own release shows how fast it moved. The portal passed 10 crore registrations on 1 December 2021, less than 100 days after its launch. About 81 per cent of the early registrations came through Common Service Centres and State Seva Kendras and 19 per cent through self-registration. About 52 per cent of those registered were women. Around 61 per cent were aged 18 to 40. Agriculture accounted for about 52 per cent of registrations, construction for about 12 per cent and domestic and household work for about 9 per cent.

The portal records occupations in about 30 broad sectors, 190 occupational families and roughly 400 occupations, based on the National Classification of Occupation. A registered worker receives an account number and an accident insurance cover of two lakh rupees under the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana from the date the policy is issued. In October 2024 the portal was upgraded into a one-stop solution. The Ministry later reported more than 31.89 crore registrations, with a single interface that connects the worker to a number of social security and welfare schemes, including the PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan pension scheme.

## Why registration matters, and what it does not do

Welfare schemes cannot reach people whom the State has not counted. A registry is therefore the first step, and the e-Shram numbers are impressive. But a registry is not a benefit. Three tests will show whether it works:

- **Is the record accurate?** Registration is largely on self-declaration, so the data have to be checked and kept up to date.
- **Are there actual benefits?** The accident insurance cover is welcome, but the unorganised worker also needs **pension, health cover, maternity benefit** and support for skills and tools.
- **Can she use it?** Benefits must be easy to claim in the worker's own language, at a nearby centre, with no need for an agent.

The 2008 Act already provides for schemes for unorganised workers and for national and State boards, but the schemes under it have been limited in scale. The Code on Social Security, 2020 brings these provisions into a wider framework and adds gig and platform workers. Whether it delivers will depend on funds and on administration.

## BMS's work here

BMS has more than a dozen federations in unorganised sectors, among them construction, beedi, agriculture, fisheries and forest workers, and these unions work in places where the formal inspector rarely goes. Their daily work is basic: helping workers obtain an identity, register for a scheme, claim a benefit and negotiate with a contractor. In November 2025 a delegation from fifteen unorganised sector federations met the Union Labour Minister on social security, a meeting this blog reports in a later post.

## What remains to be done

The long-term goals are not complicated, and they are widely shared across trade unions of different views:

- a registered, verified record for every worker;
- a minimum social security floor, including pension and health cover, that does not depend on having a formal employer;
- better enforcement of minimum wages in agriculture and construction;
- a simple grievance system close to the worker.

For BMS the goal can be put in one line: *no worker without social security.* A country cannot call itself a developed economy while nine of every ten of its workers depend on luck for their old age.
